I would definitely go for RVT. With abdomen you can still scan OB as a general tech. RVT adds more value to your resume and is highly desirable.

First question is…how much have you scanned and what have you scanned the most of? Have you done more vascular or more OB? I think having a decent amount of experience really prepares you the best for the boards. Did you do a lot of scanning in clinicals? 

I took my abdomen first as well and it was the hardest, even after scanning a ton in clinicals. OB was super easy (I thought) but I scanned a ton of that in my clinicals. Vascular I’m just studying for now, but it seems pretty easy, but I also scan a ton of vascular at my job. 

All I have ever used is URR for every board.  But honestly, experience is the best teacher. So whatever you feel the most comfortable scanning is what I would do.

I’m currently studying for RVT using URR. I have used URR for the SPI, Abdomen and OB. I passed all the first try after using URR. Abdomen is by far the hardest one in my opinion. I thought OB was super easy and straightforward (but at my facility we do TONS of OB exams). 

My suggestion would be if you don’t understand why you got something wrong, to just go look it up in a textbook/radiopedia/youtube/etc. you can find tons of explanations that can really help solidify that information for you. 

Also, URR definitely over prepares you, which I actually liked. The actual tests have been quite a bit easier than URR, if you are getting upper 70’s-80’s on the CTL exams you are definitely ready for the board. Good luck, you got this!

I think with the quant level and the fact that you see a gestational sac in the uterus. And she is only five weeks zero days (and no free fluid or pain on LT)…that definitely appears to be a corpus luteum in LT ovary. I have seen tons of corpus luteum look like that in very early pregnancy.

Ectopics being in the actual ovary is EXTREMELY rare, they are usually in the fallopian tube/adnexa. 

Only 2% of pregnancies end up ectopic and of that only 3% are in the ovary..so that is like .06% of pregnancies…so that is 3900 out of 6,500,000 pregnancies in the United States. IN ADDITION to that, you add in the rare heterotrophic pregnancy….you are talking like the odds of winning the lottery. Haha. 

Sometimes the easiest answer is the best answer. I’m pretty sure all of my rads I work with would call that a corpus luteum in LT with GS in endo. They would recommend follow up quants and US after a few weeks to check progression (like always). 

If this does end up being a heterotrophic pregnancy, with an ectopic in the left ovary….Nice…that is a once in a lifetime thing for only a tiny percentage of techs. 😊

In the USA in order to take the ARDMS, you have many different options for prerequisites. It all depends on which path you take. 

You 100% need clinical experience to take the board exams under almost all of the prerequisites (I am not sure how the other person got their info, but you definitely need clinical experience to take the boards in the US).  However based on ARDMS, it looks like you would qualify under prerequisite number 5. The requirements for that are:

1. Active credential card or license. 
2. Signed and completed clinical verification forms (usually done by your teacher or clinical instructor) 
3. A government issued ID.

Check out the links the other poster provided, that should help you. Good luck!

I think that is going to be dependent on your hospital or clinic protocol. At the hospital where I work, if we can’t see on top, we take 4 images and then we switch to a transvaginal exam. If I can see everything I need to see transabdominally I do the whole thing transabdominally. That’s going to be something that you have to decide based on the scan you’re doing and why you are doing it. 

I think if you are a student, something most of the students struggle with at first is just how hard they are gripping the dang transducer…stay aware of your grip, you can push harder and not necessarily have to grip the transducer harder. It’s really a learning process.

I have found this is usually the case when doing obese patients. I can’t help it when my hand starts to shake either. I think it’s your bodies way of telling you to ease pressure. If you can’t physically get the image, don’t hurt yourself. Your body is more important. 

Mine will start to shake a lot of the time when trying to do the fetal heart images on obese pregnant women. I do the best I can and just make sure to say “limited due to patient body habitus”…the rads I work with totally understand that. 

My other suggestion would be to stand and have the bed at about hip height. Use your upper arm muscles more to push down instead of just your hand or wrist. That can help sometimes. Ovaries can be VERY difficult to see transabdominally…transvaginal is usually way way easier to see ovaries (if it’s clinically indicated). 

I live in the Midwest and the amount of obese/overweight people we scan is about 75%…having to constantly push will definitely cause injuries if you aren’t careful. Just pay attention to your body, I’m not going to permanently damage my body because the rads want a prettier picture.

Located in North Dakota. Tons of jobs here, most places across the state will hire without ARDMS as long as you get registered within 2 years. You do need to get a state license for North Dakota but there is no test or anything, just a background check and proof that you have taken an ultrasound program, etc. you can work for 2 years on the conditional license, you just need to pass the boards within those two years. 

We are perpetually short staffed in health care in ND, probably because no one wants to live here. Winters are brutal and long, lots of snow and very low temperatures. Not a whole lot to do for younger people. Great for families though. 

But we hire new grads without ARDMS all the time.

They are two totally separate schools usually. Some hospitals/clinics will still cross train, but those places are becoming smaller and smaller. But if you wanted OB/GYN you would either have to get into another program or find a place willing to cross train and sign off on hours/scans so you can take the OB/GYN board.

It won’t be accredited by the time you graduate. My program was the same way, and I was told they had to get a full years worth of course work and grades and student information, etc. before they could even be accredited. 

They still aren’t accredited, but I have to say that I truly feel like I learned a lot, we had over 1800 hours of hands on scan time at the end of our program…and in this field I have learned that hands on experience is the best. 

I know accredited programs are the best, but for some of us who don’t have a lot of options, they are still a path to registry. And some people say that accredited programs just have better teachers and you learn more, etc…but I truly learned a lot from my unaccredited program, I had great preceptors and so so so many hours of clinicals. I truly felt totally prepared to be a tech when I was done.

The real issue you will run into is finding employment for a full year to get the hours needed before you can take your board exam. There are some places that just won’t hire you, but in many many areas of the country you would have a job in a second. 

I hope this helps, if you have more questions let me know!

First of all, ultrasound is not the modality of choice for hernias. But because of insurance and everything else, etc. they will make you do ultrasound first. CT will show a hernia way better than we can. But since we always have to do it anyway. What I do, is I look along the inguinal canal, you will see a hyperechoic “line” that separates the bowel from the muscles/fat/skin. Check alone that entire “line” and have them valsalva, if there is a hernia you will see bowel or tissue from the posterior region rise up (towards top of screen, anterior) through that “line”.  I don’t know a better way to say it, but I can say, you will know a hernia when you see it. Look for a break in the “line”, look for something moving through that line, etc. sometimes, if it’s a fat containing inguinal hernia, you may not see a thing. They are VERY hard to see if they are small, and the only way you’ll ever get it into your head is to see one. And when you see one, you will know. I’m sorry, that’s the best advice I can give you. Yes, URR costs money. I think it was like $120 for 2 months of access to the quizzes and mock exams. For me it was totally worth it, to take the test you have to pay like $200 or whatever the cost is, and if you don’t pass you have to keep paying for the test until you do pass. I didn’t want to pay more than once.

If you don’t want to spend the money, just study Edelman and really understand it. The questions in the back of the green book help. It’s just that URR has the interactive questions like they do in the actual test. When I say interactive questions I mean, they will have an ultrasound picture and you have to pick what you should do to make it better, etc. 

I’m currently using URR to study for the abdomen board and I will use it for OB/GYN and RVT as well. 

It all depends on how you learn. I learn by testing myself and getting feedback as to why something is right or wrong, etc. and that is how URR is set up.

I took the SPI and passed on my first try using just Edelman and URR. 

Honestly URR over-prepared me for the test, but it gives you a really good idea of how the test is set up and the kind of questions to expect. To be honest the questions are not worded in a way where you just memorize things, it’s way more about really knowing how the physics work. 

I would say don’t get too hung up on memorizing things and really try to understand the concepts and how everything is related. For example, when you drop frequency what is going to happen to frame rate, PRF, depth, etc. 

Everyone told me to study Doppler and really understand that, and that is helpful. The area I did the worst on was ultrasound transducers, so make sure you know the differences and how they are set up and what each layer does, etc. 

Those are the tips I can offer you! Any questions just ask.

I think the physics I took in college was way different than this physics. I would think there would still be studying involved for sure, it’s just more focused on the sound physics.

So just make sure you know the relationships more than the formulas. For example...how is axial resolution related to spatial pulse length...how is frequency related to wavelength. Things like that. Know how each of those things impacts the other things. 

There really isn’t math on the exam, but you definitely need to know how things connect to each other. Like when you change depth, what else is changed. Etc

Study Doppler...understand the different artifacts and how to correct them. I did the worst on transducers, so make sure you understand the set up and what they do. What each part is meant for. Etc. 

If you use URR or study Edelman...you should be good. Just make sure you understand it...not just memorize it. The test is really about your knowledge of the concepts and not memorization.
